backup.driveApiKeyHelpAria: How do I get a Drive API key?
backup.driveApiKeyHelpText:
Free, one-time setup. No sign-in is needed to use it:

1. Go to console.cloud.google.com and create a project (or pick an existing one).
2. APIs & Services → Library → search "Google Drive API" → Enable.
3. APIs & Services → Credentials → Create Credentials → API key.
4. Optional but recommended: restrict the key to the Drive API, and by HTTP referrer to this app's address.

Paste the key here. It can only read files in a folder you've shared as "Anyone with the link can view". It can't write, delete, or see anything else in your Drive.

challonge.heading: ☁️ Challonge
challonge.intro: Sends this tournament's roster to Challonge. For Round Robin it sends match scores too. Single Elimination, Double Elimination and Swiss send only the roster (Help explains why). You need a free Challonge developer app: sign up at connect.challonge.com for a client ID and secret. This app needs no Challonge login.
challonge.introGeneral: Push a day's games, a race or a tournament to Challonge. Each result goes once it's played, and again if it changes here. A review first shows exactly what will be sent. Round Robin and Single/Double Elimination send scores. An elimination bracket goes with its seeds, so Challonge draws the same one. Swiss sends the roster only. You need a free Challonge developer app: sign up at connect.challonge.com for a client ID and secret. No login is needed in this app.

help.allPlayers.rosterOnly: 👥 Current Roster Only — Hides everyone not on the live roster without deleting anything; turn it off to see everyone again.
help.allPlayers.show: Show — the time period the stats and graphs cover: Today, 1 Week, 1 Month, 6 Months, 1 Year, or All Time.
help.allPlayers.sortBy: Sort by — win percentage, total wins, or name.
help.allPlayers.viewToggle: 📈 See as Graph / 📊 See as Bars — Bars show Games Played/Won/Lost as scaled bars plus a timeline. Graph shows a cumulative line chart instead (see below).
help.intro: Everything the app can do, page by page. Opening Help jumps straight to the section for whatever page you're on — scroll up or down for the rest.
help.league.exportNote: Export League/Import League share a league file between devices — an imported copy is always read-only, even re-imported back onto the organizer's own device.
help.league.intro: An ongoing points ladder for a fixed group, handicapped by Skill Level. Pick APA, BCA, VNBA or TAP as the handicap system. Each player's Skill Level sets their target, so even a mismatch plays close. No server: the organizer exports a league file, and the others import it to see the standings.
help.league.queue: Queue Mode — Manual leaves each table's next pairing to the organizer. Per-Table Queue gives each table its own line. Per-Room Queue shares one line across all tables. Either way, both players from a finished match go to the back of the line instead of dropping out. When a table frees up, a confirm box (with a sound) proposes the next pairing.
help.league.setup: Setup — Create a league (8-Ball or 9-Ball), add members from your known players, and set each member's Skill Level. A suggested value comes from their app rating, and you can change it freely.
help.league.tables: Tables — Set how many tables are in play. Each gets its own slot in the Tables grid. A match that reaches its target there finishes and updates the standings by itself. Other tables' games aren't touched.
help.league.teams: Teams — Group league members into teams. Assign a team to a table (Per-Table Queue mode), and its whole roster fills that table's queue, in order. One tap keeps a team's players rotating through their table on their own.
help.main.backup: Backup & Restore — 💾 Back up now asks for a file name (today's is filled in). You can also leave out everyone's contact details. Then it saves one file with everything: players, games, stats, ratings, saved lists and settings. On a phone or tablet, you choose where it goes (Save to Files: iCloud Drive, Google Drive…). On a computer, it goes to Downloads. ⬇️ Restore a backup takes a backup file, or a link to a backup file or to a Google Drive folder of backups. Then it asks how: Add to what's here (nothing here is lost) or Replace what's here (what's here is backed up first). Recover Data undoes a reset. Share the last session sends that session to another device. Back up for a shared folder is under ⚙️ More options. (Share Standings is in Publish Daily Report.)
help.main.currentGame: Current Session — Under Tournament Setup, Load Setup applies a saved setup in one tap. Session format: 🏁 Race to N wins, or 🎯 No race. Rotate game types automatically changes the game every N games. ⏰ Timed Tournament sets a time limit instead. ⚖️ Use ratings to balance the race shortens the underdog's target by the rating gap (❓ shows the math). Current Game sets the game type, the target and its unit: racks, balls or points. The unit can differ from the game's usual one, e.g. One Pocket to "1 rack" instead of "8 balls". The ⏱️ Shot counter is here too. Reset Current Game, in ⚠️ All Resets (inside 💾 Backup & Restore), clears the live score without giving a win. ↩ Undo, above the score cards and in the win banner, takes back the last point or rack win. It restores the board exactly (scores, seats, ratings), up to 20 times. The banner's 🔄 Change winner gives the last rack to the right player. In Recent Games, ✏️ / 🗑 change any game today (winner or score) or delete it; ratings and stats follow.
help.main.gameOrder: Games Rotations — Turn on "Rotate game types automatically" to cycle through an order of game rules on its own. Each step has its own rule: game type, target number and unit (racks, balls or points). So one game type can appear twice with different rules, e.g. "8-Ball — 1 rack" then "8-Ball — 3 racks". You can edit the target and unit right in the list, any time, without removing the step. "Switch every" sets how many games are played before moving on. Load Rotation swaps in a saved order. Any new order you build is saved automatically as soon as it's set up or played.
help.main.intro: The main page is where every game is played. Each panel starts folded, with a one-line summary of what's inside. Tap the chevron to open it. The "🎨 Theme" menu at the very top changes the whole app's colours and font in one tap, and remembers your choice. There are dark, light and high-contrast themes.
help.main.players: Players — Add a player by name; it's capitalized for you. The Add button stays off until the nickname is unique. The optional "Starting rating" field gives a brand-new player a rating earned elsewhere (another league or tournament). It's ignored for anyone this device has already rated. Tap a player's Standby/Playing badge to move them in or out of the current game. ✕ removes someone from today's roster only; their career stats and rating stay. If no games were played this session yet, it doesn't ask first. 📋 Load Player List adds anyone missing from a saved list and never resets anyone already there. Export Player Lists and Import Player Lists use their own hand-editable JSON format.
help.main.ratingsNote: Ratings show as a small badge next to every player's name, all through the app. It's an Elo-style number (see Player Stats below). Each player's name is also a shortcut: tap it to open their stats page (on a roster row, tap the 📊 icon).
help.main.recentGames: Recent Games — Every game played today, newest first. A day runs from 5 a.m. to 5 a.m. So a night that goes past midnight stays one night, even when one race is won and the next begins. Last night's unsaved games stay here too. Each winner's rating change from that game shows beside their badge. The game that wins a race gets a gold highlight and its own banner ("🏆 Alice won the Race to 5 session!").
help.main.resets: All Resets — Every reset button in the app, in one place. Reset Current Game clears the live score; no win is credited. Reset Tournament offers to save any unsaved games first. Then it clears the session's wins and history and ends any active bracket tournament. Reset All Players' Official Rating puts everyone on the roster back to the default starting rating. Reset All Player Stats clears career stats and the live session. Reset Player Lists & Roster clears saved lists and the roster. Both back up first and warn you; neither touches ratings. To end only a tournament in progress, without touching the live session, use Abandon Tournament on the Tournament page. Below a dashed line at the bottom is 💀 Full Reset — Wipe Everything. It wipes the whole device back to a brand-new install: every player, rating, roster, game, tournament and setting. It asks twice and downloads a full backup first. To get anything back, you re-import that file by hand; it isn't in Recover Data like the resets above.
help.main.scoreboard: Scoreboard — The board sits above the player cards, with Focus Mode on or off. The app always opens on it (Focus Mode). The top bar has ☰ Menu, a line saying what's being played, ↩ Undo and 🎱 Game. ☰ Menu holds 🌙 End night (tonight's summary and one Share), players, tournament, league, stats, the Day Report, backups and resets, camera, recording, voice, Challonge, help, theme and language. 🎱 Game sets the game, target, race, rotation, Winner Stays, teams, timer, shot clock and practice; Apply sets them all at once. With nobody playing yet, the board offers ▶️ New game. Tap the big + on a card to score; a points game also has a small round − to take a point back. ↩ Undo takes back the last score. Reaching the target banks a win and starts the next game. ⇄ on a card swaps that player for someone on the bench. ☰ Menu › Players › Arrange the seats shows the cards' drag handles. ☰ Menu › More › Everything (the full page) brings the full page back. Numbers grow up to 3x so they read across the room, and shrink back as more players narrow the cards. Two-player games (8-Ball, 9-Ball, 10-Ball, Straight Pool, One Pocket, Snooker) turn on Winner Stays by themselves with three or more Playing. A rack then counts only for the two at the table. Winner Stays shows the winner's streak and who's next. It has no race unless you pick one (a race for each pairing), and it can cap wins in a row. Teams split A, B, A, B: one card and one + per team. Credit can pick who potted the winning ball. Practice (not saved), in 🎱 Game or Current Session, stops all saving while it's on. It asks first, and "PRACTICE · NOT SAVED" stays on the board. Wins show on screen until a reload, but nothing reaches career stats or ratings. ☰ Menu › Sounds picks All, Wins only (the default) or Off, and the volume. With Rotation on and 2 or more game types, a Rotation Position line with ◀/▶ appears under the Now Playing banner. Each tap moves the rotation one game toward its next change, like a win does. Scores, wins and ball counts don't change: it only fixes a rotation that drifted.
help.main.standings: Standings — Live race-to-N progress for teams and individuals this session.
help.main.streamOverlay: 📺 Stream overlay (OBS, YouTube, Facebook) — A see-through scoreboard over a live stream: names, ratings, score, Race to N, the game, the rack and who breaks. 1) On the scoring device (the scoreboard opened from the computer's server): ☰ Menu › More › Multi Tables › 🎯 Host This Session. 2) In OBS, add a Browser Source: URL http://localhost:4173/overlay.html?layout=lower, 1920 × 1080. For upright 9:16 video, use ?layout=vertical at 1080 × 1920. OBS on another computer: use the server computer's address instead of localhost (e.g. http://192.168.1.20:4173/overlay.html?layout=lower). Then add &device= and the app key from ☰ Menu › More › 📱 Paired devices › Show the address. 3) Go live from OBS as usual. There's nothing to tap on the overlay; options go in the address: &theme=emerald-rail (default: the scoring device's theme), &lang=french, &break=alternate (default: the last rack's winner breaks), &ratings=off, &pos=top. Full guide: docs/stream-overlay.md.
help.main.todaysNotes: Publish Daily Report — A free-text box for anything worth remembering about today's play. It saves as you type. 📋 Copy Report, 📧 Email Report and 📱 Text Report build a plain-text Day Report. It has who played, each player's wins, losses and rating change, total games and game types. Games are grouped by matchup ("Luc won 3 games of 8-Ball against Suresh"), earlier and current sessions apart. Your notes go in too.
help.playerPage.exportReset: 💾 Save to history copies this player's games from the live session into their saved history. Reset Stats clears only this player's saved history. Their rating is untouched: it's stored separately and never reset from here.
help.playerPage.graph: Graph — The same cumulative games chart as All Players, scoped to this one player, plus the standalone Rating chart underneath.
help.playerPage.h2h: Head-to-Head — A folded panel (tap to open) with a win/loss record against each opponent faced in the chosen period. Its summary line lists who they've played, without opening it.
help.playerPage.intro: Opened by tapping a player's name anywhere in the app.
help.playerPage.liveSession: This Session (Live) — What they've done in the game currently in progress.
help.playerPage.ratingsAbout: About ratings: every player has a rating, the app's own Elo-style number (roughly 0–900). With a 100-point gap, the higher-rated player is expected to win about 2 games for every 1. Each further 100 points doubles those odds. New players start at 400, unless you gave a starting rating when adding them (see Players, above). That only seeds a brand-new name; it can't change a rating already being tracked. After that, the rating updates itself after every credited game, on the main scoreboard or in a tournament. It can't be edited by hand. Both players in a game move by the same amount. A new player moves faster and a regular slower, so the two speeds are averaged. Team games count too, each side by its average rating. A league match counts once. A game of several racks, or of Straight Pool, counts up to three times as much as a single rack. The rating badge follows each player's name all through the app.
help.camera.intro: An optional feature: a camera watches the table and selects the right player on the keypad when they bend over to shoot. The camera can be a separate phone mounted over the table, or this tablet's own camera (built-in or USB). It knows people by clothing and rough body shape, not faces. So each player needs a quick one-time "enrollment", and a little upkeep to stay accurate. This section covers all of it.
help.camera.setup: Setup — Open "Visual Scoring" under the score cards, or tap "📷 Set Up Camera" at the top. In "Select Camera", pick a separate phone (local network only, no internet) or this tablet's own camera. This device's camera needs a secure page (HTTPS or localhost); the setup block says if that's missing. Once set up, the camera starts on its own, minimized in Visual Scoring, every time the page loads.
help.camera.calibration: Calibrating the table — This shows the camera where your rails are, so it only counts people at the table. Someone walking past or sitting nearby isn't counted. Tap "⛶ Full Screen" on the camera preview. Tap the 4 corners yourself (most reliable), or try "Detect table automatically". That's faster, but tricky light or reflections can make it misread the cloth color. Then turn on "👁️ Show camera debug info during play". The pink outline should trace your real table; if it doesn't, calibrate again before trusting anything else.
help.camera.enroll: Enrollment — A player not yet enrolled has an "Enroll" button in the roster. It opens the camera's player list. There, press Identify while the player is at the table, and Shooting while they're down on a shot. Each press adds a sample, any time, even mid-game. Each row has a self-check: how often the camera recognizes them, and who it confuses them with. Samples that look like someone else can be removed there. The camera uses clothing colours and an appearance model; the self-check picks whichever works better tonight. Until a player has 20 samples from those buttons today, every point you confirm for them also teaches the camera. So select the right player on the keypad before you confirm each point. After that, only the buttons add samples. If a player changes shirts, press Identify and Shooting for them a few times. On a new day (from 5 a.m.), the camera still knows everyone by trousers, cap or hair, build and how they shoot. It only relearns their shirt, the same way. With a number pad: during play, select a player by number, then 7 = seen, 8 = shooting, 0 = take back the last one. On the camera's Enroll tab: player number = seen, + = shooting, - = take back. Tap the "?" beside an enrolled player's icon for the full explanation.
help.camera.scorecardIcons: Scorecard icons — Once the camera is set up, a camera icon sits above each player's name on the scorecard. Its colour shows what the camera knows about them right now. Green: in view and recognized by how they look. Yellow: someone in view is taken for them, but not for sure (followed along their path, a near match, a best guess). Blue: out of view, but the camera has an idea where they are (held at the table, or where it last saw them). Light grey: not seen, nothing to go on. A "+" means a new sample was just captured for them. A "?" means the camera sees someone bent over that it can't name for sure, and this is its best guess. Tap that player on the keypad to confirm. This also gives the camera a strong, human-confirmed sample.
help.camera.unmatchedBanner: "Select player from keypad" banner — Shows under the scorecards when the camera sees someone shooting and can't tell who. It clears by itself once resolved. Tap the real shooter on the keypad to dismiss it and tell the camera who it was, like the "?" icon above.
help.camera.settings: Tuning settings — These tune the camera: Match sensitivity, Consecutive frames required, Re-announce after, the two Bent-over angles and Max distance from the rail. They're in Visual Scoring > ⚙️ Capture Settings, and in the camera's own Settings tab. They apply to this tablet's camera or a separate camera phone. Each has a "?" that says in plain words what raising or lowering it does.
help.camera.troubleshootNote: If recognition seems unreliable, turn on "👁️ Show camera debug info during play". The running log under the checkbox shows the real distance numbers behind every miss. That beats guessing which setting to change. Camera placement matters more than any setting. Mount it along one of the table's long sides, not at one end. That roughly halves how much a player's size and sharpness change as they move around. Calibration, enrollment and settings survive restarts, and are in every backup like everything else.
help.playerPage.sessionHistory: Session History — Every past saved session, expandable into the individual games played.
help.playerPage.synopsis: Stats Synopsis — Rating (the current number) and "Rating this period" (how much it moved). Also Wins, Losses and Win %, for Today, Last 7 Days, Last 30 Days, This Year or All Time.
help.title: ❓ Help & Guide
help.tournament.careerNote: Every rack played in a tournament still counts toward career stats, ratings, and the All Players graphs — it isn't a separate pool of data.
help.tournament.format: Format — Double Elimination: lose once and you drop to the losers bracket; lose twice and you're out. Single Elimination: lose once and you're out. It's the fastest, with no losers bracket or grand final. Round Robin: no elimination; everyone plays everyone once. When every match is done, whoever has the most match wins is champion, and a tie at the top is shared. Swiss: no elimination either, but not every pairing is played. Each round pairs players with similar records, for a fixed number of rounds. Whoever has the most match wins at the end is champion.
help.tournament.intro: A knockout bracket — or a round robin — instead of a regular session.
help.tournament.reading: Reading the bracket — Winners Bracket, Losers Bracket (double elimination only) and Grand Final show as a sideways tree with connecting lines. The active match is highlighted, eliminated players are crossed out, and the champion gets a 👑. Round Robin and Swiss instead show live Standings - match wins, then head-to-head, rack difference and racks won - above their matches; nobody is crossed out there. Every finished match shows its score. 📺 shows the live match or the bracket full screen, for a TV.
help.tournament.setup: Setup — Pick a format: tap the ❓ next to one to see what it means, then "✅ Yes, this format". Then pick the game type, and the target and race for each match. Under Players, "🎲 Random selection" draws the field at random. "🔢 Set seed manually" lets you rank it; a blank seed keeps the checklist's order. Round robin matches always come in random order, since there's no bracket to seed.
help.wizard.cancelNote: Canceling is always safe. Players you added and rotation changes you made are already saved, just as if you'd used the main page panels.
help.wizard.intro: The fastest way to start playing. Five steps, each with its own on-screen explanation:
help.wizard.quickCounterNote: ⏱️ Only a temporary counter — Tick it on Step 1 and a "▶️ Start Game Now" button appears. Tapping it skips the rest of the wizard and opens a bare point counter in Focus Mode. There's no game type, no target, no rotation and no win/loss detection. Nothing is saved: stats, ratings and saved lists are all gone when you reload. You can edit any card's name, each card has its own remove button, and scores can go negative. An "+ Add Player" field sits at the end of the row. If there's a saved player list, a "📋 Load Player List" row appears too. Loading one makes the active players match that list exactly. Anyone not on it goes to standby; their data isn't lost, and typing their name again brings them back. "↺ Reset All to 0" sets every card to 0 at once, with no confirmation. Everything you need is right there on the scoreboard.
help.wizard.step1: 1. Game type & format — Individual (casual, no fixed target), Race To (asks for a win target), or Tournament Elimination (skips straight to the bracket setup below).
help.wizard.step2: 2. Players — Load a saved list and/or add players; each chip has a ✕ to remove someone you don't want in this game.
help.wizard.step3: 3. Playing vs Standby — Turn on Playing for everyone in this game (at least two required to continue).
help.wizard.step4: 4. Rotation — Plain yes/no: automatically switch game types, or just play one type all session.
help.wizard.step5: 5. Review & Start — A summary of every choice; Start applies it all, switches to Focus Mode, and closes the wizard.

Players with fewer than {{minGames}} games aren't ranked. Tournament wins, dominant wins, skunk wins and long runs all count extra.

league.handicapChartExplainFixed: This is APA's real, fixed nationwide chart — the same everywhere, so there's nothing to edit here. Each player's own Skill Level sets their target directly.

The higher-rated player's race is the one that makes the match closest to even, by the app's ratings. 100 rating points = winning 2 games in 3. Their race is at most {{max}}; past that, race length alone can't even out the match. The table shows the race at a range of rating gaps.

league.handicapHelp: With handicap on, the chosen system's chart sets each match's race. APA 8-Ball uses both players' Skill Levels together. APA 9-Ball (and VNBA/TAP, as you enter them) uses each player's own. Anyone the chart doesn't cover uses the base number instead. For BCA/VNBA/TAP, that means every player until you add your own league's numbers. With handicap off, everyone races to the base number, with no handicap.
league.handicapSystemInfoText:
Not sure which to pick? Here's the difference.

APA publishes official nationwide charts, the same everywhere. In 8-Ball, both players' Skill Levels together set the race (a 7 against a 6 is 5–4). In 9-Ball, each player's own Skill Level sets the points they need. The app already has APA's real charts built in.

BCA, VNBA and TAP work differently. Each local league sets its own numbers (for TAP, a computer works them out from recent play). So there's no single official chart to build in. If you pick one of these, add your league's numbers under Tables → Base Games to Win. Add the Skill Level chart too, if your league posts one. The app then uses those instead of guessing.

Still deciding? APA is the safe default: it's the only one with real numbers from the start.

playerPage.ratingKExplain:
Every player starts at a rating of 400. After each game, the winner's rating goes up and the loser's goes down. Two things decide by how much:

1. How surprising the result was. Beating someone rated much higher moves your rating more than beating someone you were expected to beat.

2. The "K" number shown here, which sets how fast a rating can change. New players (under 20 games) use K=24, so their rating catches up to their real skill quickly. After that, K drops to 8, so one odd result doesn't swing it much.

players.cameraInputHelpAria: What does camera player recognition do?
players.cameraInputHelpText:
When this is on, a camera watches the table and confirms or corrects the player selected on the keypad. It can be a separate phone or tablet over the table, or this tablet's own camera (USB or built-in). Set either one up with the 📷 Set Up Camera button.

A two-device setup only works on your local network. No internet or cloud is involved.
players.cameraMatchThresholdHelpText:
How close the camera's best guess must be to count as a match. It uses the same distance units as the debug log (e.g. "closest: Elena (1.87, need ≤1.20)"). Lower = stricter: fewer wrong matches, but a real match can be rejected as "too far". Higher = looser: real matches come more easily, but different players can get mixed up.

Turn on "Show camera debug info during play" and watch the closest-match distance in the log while someone shoots. If it's always just a bit over this number, raise it a little. If it's far higher (3x or more), the problem is the enrollment, not this setting. Enroll that player again instead.
players.cameraDebounceSecHelpText: Once the camera confirms a player is shooting, it waits this many seconds before confirming that player again. So several shots in a row don't keep re-selecting them or repeating their voice announcement. Lower it if turns are fast. Raise it if one visit to the table means a long run of shots.
players.cameraDebugEnable: 👁️ Show camera debug info during play
players.cameraDebugEnableHelpAria: What does Show camera debug info do?
players.cameraDebugEnableHelpText: Shows a live status line and a running log under this checkbox: exactly what the camera detects. You see whether it sees a pose, upright or bent over, and the angle. You also see the closest enrolled player's name and distance, even without an official match. Turn this on when recognition seems not to work, to see which part fails instead of guessing.
players.cameraVoiceEnableHelpAria: What does Speak player status do?
players.cameraVoiceEnableHelpText: Reads status out loud from this device. It says "[Name] seen" when the camera recognizes someone standing at the table. It says "[Name] shooting" once a shot is confirmed. Useful when you're not looking at the screen. Both need a real match, so if matching isn't working yet (see the debug log), you'll hear nothing. During play, it doesn't name each player the camera switches to; that was constant chatter. It does only while "Show camera debug info during play" or Cue debug mode is ticked. In Straight Pool, it also names a shot the camera is at least 80% sure of. The debug log shows how sure each one was. Pressing Identify or Shooting flashes that player's score card instead: once for seen, twice for shooting.
players.cameraRemoteCalibrateHelpAria: What does Calibrate Table Remotely do?
players.cameraRemoteCalibrateHelpText: Calibrate the table from this screen instead of walking over to the camera phone. Tap the button and a live still from the camera appears here. Tap each corner of the table in the image, one at a time, going around in order, as you would on the phone. This only works with a separate camera phone (cross-device mode). This tablet's own camera already shows its calibration screen directly.
players.cameraRemoteViewerHelpAria: What does Full Camera Setup (Remote) do?
players.cameraRemoteViewerHelpText: Opens the camera device's full setup screen right here, so you don't have to walk over. Table calibration, enrolling players and recognition settings: the same controls as at the camera phone itself. Tap anything in this window as you would on the phone; it really happens there. Only camera permission must be granted on the phone itself, the first time. Everything after that can be done from here.
players.cameraBallTrackingEnable: 🎱 Ball tracking (Straight Pool): auto-credit pocketed balls
players.cameraBallTrackingHelpText: In Straight Pool, the camera counts the balls on the calibrated table between shots. When a ball disappears for good, the selected shooter gets the point. A missing cue ball is announced as a scratch (-1). This needs the camera's own "Ball tracking" setting on too, and a calibrated table (that's where the pocket positions come from). Nothing counts while balls move, a player is bent over, or a cue or arm lies on the cloth. If it credits a ball that wasn't pocketed, press - on the keypad; if it misses one, press +. Both corrections teach the camera how patient to be. Re-racks and balls reappearing from under a hand are announced, never scored.

players.cameraCueDebugHelpAria: What does Cue debug mode do?
players.cameraCueDebugHelpText: Shows exactly what the camera's cue detection is doing. Each time a cue comes out, is put away, or is given to a player, the log below these checkboxes adds a line. The camera's video shows the cue drawn in pink, with its length and who it was matched to. When "Speak player status" is on, you also hear "Cue detected on table". If a cue comes out and nobody in view is holding it, the last player the camera saw is set as shooting. The log says so. It doesn't change what gets detected. Turn it off for normal play.

players.cameraMatchSliderHelpText:
How closely someone must look like an enrolled player before the camera gives them that name.

0 = never names anyone. 3 = the default. 6 = names everyone as their closest enrolled player, however different they look.

Lower = fewer wrong names. But a real player can go unrecognized if the light or their clothes changed a bit since enrollment.

Higher = recognizes real players more easily, but starts mixing players up.

Move it one step at a time: up if someone keeps going unrecognized, down if players get mixed up. Re-enrolling a player usually helps more than any setting.

players.cameraConsecutiveFramesHelpAria: What does Consecutive frames required do?
players.cameraConsecutiveFramesHelpText:
How many detection frames in a row must agree before the camera trusts what it sees: a stance change, a steady match, a shot.

Lower = reacts faster, but one bad or blurry frame can fool it more easily.

Higher = slower to react, but steadier, with fewer false triggers.

If switching players feels slow, lower it a bit. If it fires on brief glitches, raise it.
players.cameraBendEnterHelpAria: What does the bent-over enter angle do?
players.cameraBendEnterHelpText:
How many degrees a player's upper body must tip forward from upright before the camera decides they're bending over to shoot.

Lower = catches a short, shallow bend sooner, but just leaning in can set it off.

Higher = needs a deeper, clearer bend. Fewer false triggers, but a quick, shallow shot can be missed. A cue held out over the table counts as shooting, whatever this angle reads.
players.cameraBendExitHelpAria: What does the back-to-upright angle do?
players.cameraBendExitHelpText:
How far a player must straighten up before the camera counts them as upright again.

Keep it below the enter angle. That gap stops the reading flickering while someone holds about the same lean.

Closer to the enter angle = notices standing up sooner, but flickers more. Lower = steadier, but slower to notice.
players.cameraRailDistanceHelpAria: What does Max distance from the rail do?
players.cameraRailDistanceHelpText:
How far from the nearest table edge someone can stand and still count as "at the table". Only used once the table is calibrated.

Lower = stricter. Only someone right at the rail counts, but a player standing back to line up a shot can be missed.

Higher = more forgiving, but someone walking past nearby is more likely to count.
players.cameraBallConfirm: Still passes before a pocketed ball counts
players.cameraBallConfirmHelpAria: What does Still passes before a pocketed ball counts do?
players.cameraBallConfirmHelpText:
Ball tracking only: the camera takes still looks at the table, about one a second. This sets how many in a row must agree a ball is gone before it's credited.

Lower = credits faster, but a ball hidden for a moment by a hand or glare may count as pocketed.

Higher = slower and steadier. The keypad tunes this itself. A - right after an automatic credit raises it; a + for a missed ball lowers it.
players.cameraCueDetectionHelpAria: What does Cue stick detection do?
players.cameraCueDetectionHelpText:
Looks for a cue held out over the calibrated table. A player at the table with their cue over the cloth is taking a shot. This counts even when the camera can't see them bend over.

If a player drops out of view right next to the table, they're assumed to be still there. The next cue that comes out is credited to them. When nobody can be named at all, the last player the camera saw in the past 2 minutes is set as shooting.

Needs the table to be calibrated.
players.cameraWalkingPathsHelpAria: What does Follow walking paths do?
players.cameraWalkingPathsHelpText:
Follows the path each person walks around the room. A recognized player may drop out of view: behind someone else, behind the lamp, or out of the picture. If someone turns up along their path (or right where they vanished) within about 12 seconds, it's taken to be them. That person keeps the player's name.

If that person clearly looks like a different enrolled player, the camera goes by their looks instead. If two players vanish close together and it can't tell which one came back, it doesn't guess.

Works best with the table calibrated.
players.cameraEnrollHelpText:
Enrolling teaches the camera what a player looks like (their clothes, not their face), so it can recognize them during play.

Tap Enroll to open the camera's player list. Each player has two buttons. Press Identify while they're at the table: the camera learns their clothing colours, rough body shape and where they stand. Press Shooting while they're down on a shot: it also learns how they shoot. Each press adds a sample, as many as you like, even mid-game.

Until a player has 20 button samples today, each point you confirm for them on the keypad also adds a sample. That keeps up with a shirt change or new lighting. So select the right player on the keypad before each point, ideally every shot. After 20 button samples today, only the buttons add more, so the camera's own guesses can't teach it a mistake. If they change shirts then, press Identify and Shooting for them a few times.

On a new day (from 5 a.m.) there's nothing to redo. The camera keeps what it learned: trousers, cap or hair, build, how they shoot, where they stand. It relearns only the shirt, from the first Identify press or confirmed point of the day. Until then it goes by the rest.

The player list also runs a self-check on each player. It shows how often their own samples recognize them and who they get mixed up with. It flags any sample that looks more like someone else, with a button to remove it. Two players dressed alike are named only when the camera is sure. It recognizes players by clothing colours and by an appearance model trained on thousands of people. It uses whichever the self-check finds better.

tournament.formatDouble:
Winners & Losers Brackets: lose once and you drop to the losers bracket for a second chance. Lose twice and you're out.

Fairer than single elimination, since one bad game doesn't end your tournament. But it takes longer to play.
tournament.formatRoundRobin:
No elimination: everyone plays everyone else once.

Most match wins takes it. Level on wins: head-to-head, then rack difference, then racks won; still level at the top, a playoff or a shared title. Best for a casual group where everyone should play the same number of games.
tournament.formatSingle:
Only winners advance: lose once and you're out.

The fastest format — best for a quick knockout when there isn't time for a longer event.
tournament.formatSwiss:
No one is knocked out. Everyone plays a set number of rounds (e.g. 4 or 5). Each round, you're drawn against an opponent with the same win-loss record - never the same one twice while the draw allows it.

When those rounds are done, most match wins takes the title; level on wins: head-to-head, rack difference, racks won.

keypad.speechHelpText:
🔊 When this is on, the app speaks when you switch players with the keypad (number keys 1-9, Enter). It also speaks when + or - puts someone in the lead. Handy when you can't look at the screen.

Switching to a new player (keypad, or a tap on their card): "[Previous player], total [count] points" (if someone was selected), then "[New player] Playing, [count] points". It adds ", Leader" if that player is already ahead.

When a point puts someone in the lead: "[Name] takes the lead". Only at that moment, not on every point while they stay ahead.

Tapping + or - on a player's own card also selects that player, and always speaks the change. If they were already selected: "plus/minus [count] point". If the tap just selected them: "[Name] plus/minus [count] point". In rack games (8-Ball, 9-Ball, etc.), a + that reaches the target says "[Name] won the game" instead. That's only when the tap just selected them; if the winner was already selected, it stays silent.

The "Voice" list shows only the voices installed on this device. If none of its voices is installed, it uses Siri (the device's best default voice).

players.cameraZoomHelpText:
Zooms in on the middle of the camera's picture. Use it when the table looks small, with too much room around it. When zoomed, the camera is asked for more pixels (1080p, then 4K if it has it), so the picture keeps its detail.

The zoom stays centred, so aim the camera at the middle of the table. The table calibration is converted for you; no need to calibrate again. But the empty-room snapshot has to be taken again.

players.cameraFlip180HelpText:
For a camera hung upside down (from the ceiling or under a shelf). Turns its picture the right way up, on screen and for player and ball recognition.

The table calibration is converted for you. The empty-room snapshot must be taken again.
players.cameraBallSensitivityHelpAria: What does Ball detection sensitivity do?
players.cameraBallSensitivityHelpText:
How different from empty felt a spot must be to count as a ball. With an empty-room snapshot (camera page, Table tab), each spot of cloth is compared with the same spot in the snapshot. Its lights and shadows count as empty felt. Without one, it's compared with the felt's single colour.

1 = only clear differences count. Fewer false balls (shadows, chalk, glare), but a ball close to the felt's colour can be missed. 10 = the slightest difference counts. A green ball on green felt is found, but so may be a shadow. 5 is the standard.

On the camera page (Table tab), the slider shows the result live on the picture.
